questions.q: What is a node, in the context of a blockchain?
options: A type of cryptocurrency wallet only
A single transaction recorded on the chain
A physical server owned exclusively by one company
An object on the network that stores and transmits ledger information
questions.explain: A node is both a holder and a beacon of information — it keeps a copy of the ledger and helps broadcast transactions across the network.

questions.q: Which node type is a typical wallet app like MetaMask an example of?
options: A block explorer
A full node
A snapshot (light) node
An archive node
questions.explain: Wallet apps generally connect as snapshot/light nodes — just enough to broadcast a transaction without storing the network's full historical detail.

questions.q: Why are nodes tiered into different types (snapshot, full, archive) at all?
options: It's a random historical accident with no real reason
Tiering exists purely to slow down block explorers
It's a direct result of scalability — storing full detail everywhere would make running the network far more expensive
Only archive nodes are allowed to send transactions
questions.explain: Since every transaction costs money to verify and reward, tiering node detail levels keeps the network's overall cost of operation manageable.

The physical file size of a single block
How many nodes exist on the network
The number of transactions inside one specific block
questions.explain: Block height is the last recorded count of blocks produced — effectively a measure of how long the blockchain has been running.

questions.q: What is a block explorer used for?
options: Writing Solidity smart contracts
Storing a user's private keys
Acting as a website front end to look up real transactions and ledger data
Mining new blocks directly
questions.explain: EtherScan (Ethereum) and Bitquery (multi-chain) are real examples — they let anyone view the ledger without running their own node.
